prompt: The client asks: "Should the city build a new bus line or improve existing routes?" Fact sheet: a new line costs $50M and would serve 8,000 riders a day; upgrading existing routes costs $20M and cuts trip times 20% for 40,000 riders a day; ridership fell 15% as trips slowed; city hall was renovated last year. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Upgrades cost $20M and speed up trips 20% for 40,000 daily riders, against $50M for 8,000 on a new line, so improving existing routes should come first.
options.feedback: The reasoning is right, but the answer comes last. Lead with the recommendation.

options.text: Build the new line. It brings service to 8,000 riders a day who have none, and new lines win riders in a way repairs don't.
options.feedback: It ignores cost and cause: $50M for 8,000 riders, while slow trips are why 15% of riders left.

options.text: Improve existing routes first: for $20M, trips will get 20% faster for 40,000 daily riders, against $50M for 8,000 on a new line.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and backs it with cost per rider and the cause of the decline.

options.text: Improve existing routes. Having renovated city hall last year, the city needs to show riders visible results this year.
options.feedback: City hall's renovation has nothing to do with buses. Cost per rider and the cause of the decline support the answer.

explanation: Full answer: Improve existing routes first. For $20M, upgrades make trips 20% faster for 40,000 daily riders, against $50M for a new line serving 8,000, and slow trips are why ridership fell 15%. The main risk is that faster trips don't win riders back, so the next step is to upgrade the busiest routes first and measure ridership. What would change the answer: ridership staying flat on the upgraded routes.

irrelevant_facts: City hall was renovated last year.
